title: Success and continuity
lines: The Society That Selects Us examines a paradox inside modern success.
A society can reward education while making family life harder to sustain.
This scientific and philosophical essay follows that tension through fertility, personality, and institutions.
It separates genetic change from cultural transmission, social filtering, and demographic shifts.
That separation helps readers examine selection without mistaking every social change for biological destiny.

title: The same wish
lines: Chapter four compares people who express the same wish for two children.
One has nearby grandparents, affordable housing, and a predictable working day.
The other faces expensive rent, repeated moves, and a long commute.
The difference lies between wanting a family and having room to realize it.
The book calls attention to compatibilities between personal traits and institutional arrangements.

sentenceDirection.visualAction: two inhabited domestic cutaways of equal size and equal dignity; a shared handwritten family wish is represented by two blank future place settings, not children appearing or disappearing. Left: a grandparent passes a school satchel to a parent at a nearby home entrance; a short workday strip leaves open evening space. Right: a moving carton remains half-unpacked, a bus crosses a visibly longer route, and the travel portion consumes the evening interval. At the payoff the long travel strip recedes enough to show the obstructed family-time region; no invented successful family or birth is shown. Same wish, different time budget is enacted. Each cast member has motivated gaze, handoff and posture rather than background bobbing.

title: Rebuilding the distance
lines: Those barriers become the starting point for the book's four possible futures.
One scenario redraws the city around nearby housing, schools, work, and care.
A second child would no longer necessarily require another exhausting move.
The proposed change supports family choices while preserving different professions and ways of living.
This metropolis of proximity is a scenario to examine, not a guaranteed forecast.
The wider comparison asks which freedoms each social arrangement preserves or puts under pressure.

sentenceDirection.visualAction: a large practical tabletop city model, viewed in oblique elevation, with the original study characters now acting as planners/inhabitants. A parent holds a satchel while a planner moves the care building into the open courtyard near housing; the long bus route contracts into a walkable connection. School, workshop and housing retain recognizably different architectural uses. The second place setting from scene 2 can fit on the table without moving the household itself; no actual additional child is produced. A small hinged plan page marked Scenario stays visible. Last beat opens the adjacent model leaves only as alternative spatial organizations—dense tower, clustered enclaves, algorithmic matching interface—without pretending to prove their outcomes. Foreground palette is lively, simple background; all labels above caption-safe region.

title: Read the mechanisms
lines: The book also examines personality measurement, migration, and the limits of demographic evidence.
Its evidence appendix distinguishes supported findings from hypotheses and possible tests.
That matters when a claim about groups starts sounding like an individual destiny.
The closing argument favors fewer arbitrary barriers, rather than prescribing anyone's family size.
Begin with chapter four, then compare its filters with the metropolis of proximity.
Read for the connections between everyday institutions and the human diversity they can sustain.
